summary.text: Hund's rule predicts the ground state of an atom or molecule that has one or more open electronic shells.
It says that when orbitals of equal energy are available, electrons occupy them singly with the same spin before filling them in pairs.
Friedrich Hund discovered it in 1925, and it is used in atomic chemistry, spectroscopy and quantum chemistry.

facts.label: Multiplicity
facts.value: The number of unpaired electrons plus 1

facts.label: Nitrogen's ground state
facts.value: Three unpaired electrons of parallel spin, multiplicity 4

facts.label: Oxygen's 2p⁴ electrons
facts.value: One orbital holds a pair, and two hold one each

facts.label: Manganese's 3d⁵
facts.value: Five unpaired electrons, all of parallel spin

items.prompt: Four electrons settle into three orbitals of equal energy. How are they arranged?

options.label: Two orbitals hold a pair each and the third stays empty
One orbital holds a pair and the other two hold one each
Each orbital holds one, and the fourth electron goes elsewhere
All four stack into the first orbital before the others

items.explain: Before any two electrons share an orbital, the others in the subshell must each hold one, so only one orbital ends up with a pair, as in oxygen's 2p⁴.

items.prompt: A nitrogen atom's ground state has three unpaired electrons of parallel spin. What is its multiplicity?
items.explain: The multiplicity is the number of unpaired electrons plus 1, which gives 4 for three unpaired electrons.

items.prompt: A textbook says electrons spread across separate orbitals because they push each other apart. What have accurate calculations since the 1970s shown?

options.label: Spreading out cuts the screening of the nucleus's pull on the electrons
Spreading out lets the electrons pack in more tightly
The push between electrons is stronger when they are apart
Spreading out has no effect on how stable the atom is

items.explain: The early explanation was incorrect: the real reason is less screening of electron-nuclear attraction, so unpaired electrons can approach the nucleus more closely.

items.prompt: The two electrons in oxygen's two equal-energy outer molecular orbitals could instead sit together in one orbital. How does that version compare with the ground state?

options.label: It is an even lower state, so it is the ground state
It is the same state under another name
It is an excited state and is more reactive
It is a state that cannot exist for oxygen

items.explain: The ground state has two unpaired electrons in singly occupied orbitals, while singlet oxygen with one doubly occupied and one empty orbital is an excited state with greater reactivity.

items.prompt: A chemist says an atom's ground state is a high-spin state. What does that tell you?

options.label: It has many unpaired electrons with parallel spin
All of its electrons are paired up in orbitals
Its electrons are spinning around the nucleus fastest
It has few unpaired electrons with opposite spins

items.explain: A high-multiplicity state is the same as a high-spin state, and the lowest-energy state with maximum multiplicity usually has unpaired electrons all with parallel spin.

items.prompt: The Aufbau principle tells you which subshell fills next. What does Hund's rule add?

options.label: Which element the next subshell belongs to in the table
How electrons spread over that subshell's equal-energy orbitals
How many protons the atom must hold to stay stable
Which of all the subshells carries the highest energy

items.explain: Hund's rule places constraints on how orbitals fill in the ground state: each orbital in a subshell gets one electron before any gets a second.

paragraphs.heading: The rule
paragraphs.text: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity predicts the ground state of an atom or molecule that has one or more open electronic shells, and it rests on observations of atomic spectra. Within a subshell, electrons first go in one per orbital, all with the same spin, and only then start to pair up. Put simply, when several orbitals share the same energy, electrons spread out across them before doubling up. Friedrich Hund found the rule in 1925, and it is an important tool in atomic chemistry, spectroscopy and quantum chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: Counting multiplicity
paragraphs.text: The multiplicity of a state is 2S + 1, where S is the total electronic spin, so high multiplicity means high spin. Each electron has a spin of 1/2, so the total spin equals half the count of unpaired electrons, and the multiplicity is one more than that count. Nitrogen's ground state, for example, has three unpaired electrons with parallel spin, giving a total spin of 3/2 and a multiplicity of 4.

paragraphs.heading: Why it lowers the energy
paragraphs.text: The high-spin arrangement is lower in energy and more stable because its unpaired electrons have parallel spin, and the Pauli exclusion principle forces them into different orbitals. An early explanation said that spreading out kept electrons farther apart and cut their repulsion, but that turned out to be wrong. Accurate quantum-mechanical calculations since the 1970s show the real reason: the electrons screen each other less from the nucleus, so they can get closer to it and feel a stronger attraction.

paragraphs.heading: Filling orbitals
paragraphs.text: Hund's rule puts limits on how orbitals fill in the ground state under the Aufbau principle. Every orbital in a subshell must hold one electron before any orbital takes a second. The electrons in a subshell also line up with parallel spin before opposite-spin electrons start to be added. The result is that filling always gives the largest possible number of unpaired electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Examples in atoms
paragraphs.text: In oxygen, the four electrons of the 2p subshell sit as [↑↓] [↑] [↑], not as [↑↓] [↑] [↓] or [↑↓] [↑↓] [ ]. Manganese, with a 3d⁵ configuration, has five unpaired electrons all with parallel spin, which gives a ⁶S ground state; the 6 is the multiplicity. Chromium is the lightest atom with a ground state that has two partly filled subshells close in energy. Its 3d⁵4s configuration has six unpaired parallel-spin electrons and a ⁷S ground state.

paragraphs.heading: Molecules and exceptions
paragraphs.text: Most stable molecules have closed electron shells, but a few have unpaired electrons, and Hund's rule applies to them. The key example is the oxygen molecule, O₂, which has two antibonding orbitals of equal energy holding just two electrons. Following the rule, its ground state is triplet oxygen, with those two electrons unpaired in separate orbitals. The singlet state, with both in one orbital, is an excited state that is more reactive. In 2004 researchers made 5-dehydro-m-xylylene, the first organic molecule known to break Hund's rule.
